entries.fact: Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919), biologist and artist, filled Kunstformen der Natur with organisms drawn as ornament. In the room's canon he is Davis's ancestor: the creatures are built the way he drew — many layered marks, symmetry as construction.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: George Lois (1931–2022), the advertising art director of the Big Idea. The room's judge works in his register; the maxims in this bank are paraphrases of his philosophy in KC-1's own words — the homage is the thinking, never a quotation.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson (1860–1948), mathematician and biologist: On Growth and Form argued that a living shape is a diagram of the forces that made it. The room keeps it as its oldest book.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: Georgy Voronoy (1868–1908), mathematician. His diagram gives every seed the territory nearest to it; the room's fields, dishes and weathers are drawn inside that idea.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: Floyd–Steinberg dithering diffuses each pixel's quantising error to its neighbours, so a coarse grid keeps a picture's tone. The room's faces take the other road — Bayer's — but the argument is the same.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: The Met's impression of Hokusai's Great Wave — Under the Wave off Kanagawa, from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji — is a woodblock print in ink and colour on paper, dated about 1830–32.
entries.rights: CC0 — The Met Open Access (object data)

entries.fact: On Growth and Form, D'Arcy Thompson's study of shape in living things, was published in 1917 — biology written as mathematics, a century before the room's creatures.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: Ordered dithering tests each pixel against a repeating threshold pattern; Bayer's matrix is the pattern the room's faces are ground through — tone from almost nothing.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: A Voronoi diagram partitions a plane into cells, one around each seed, every point in a cell nearer its seed than any other. It is geometry the room computes with constantly.
entries.rights: CC0 — Wikidata structured facts (no Wikipedia text)

entries.fact: Lois's first rule, in paraphrase: the big idea comes first — execution is only its delivery, and decoration standing where an idea should be is an apology.
entries.rights: Original KC-1 wording paraphrasing the philosophy (05 homage boundary); no source text reproduced

entries.fact: Lois's method, in paraphrase: creativity is not decoration but problem-solving — find the one true thing about the work and say it so plainly it cannot be unheard.
entries.rights: Original KC-1 wording paraphrasing the philosophy (05 homage boundary); no source text reproduced

entries.fact: Lois's test of the work, in paraphrase: if it makes nobody nervous, it is wallpaper — the room would rather be argued with than upholstered.
entries.rights: Original KC-1 wording paraphrasing the philosophy (05 homage boundary); no source text reproduced
